To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we derived the deterministic lattice equations governing diffusion in inohomogeneous media, and found that the fraction of particles in each domain depends only on the number of sites in the domain, the number of particles, the particle hopping rate, and the number of species.

the steady-state particle number at a given lattice site in an inhomogeneous system is independent of the arrangement and shape, and only depends (1) on the number of distinct species in the system and (2) on the number and size of the spatial domains.

the steady-state particle distribution for diffusion in inhomogenous media only depends on the total number of lattice sites, the number of lattice site types, the hopping rates between neighboring lattice sites, and the number of particles of a given species.

the development and analysis of a new computational approach, the DLEs, for the prediction of the (average) spatial distributions of randomly diffusing (single- or multi-) particle species in inhomogeneous systems.

the distribution of randomly diffuting particles in inhomogoneous media can be predicted from the lattice equations.

the DLEs provide, for diffusion in inhomogeneously structured systems, a deterministic and computationally efficient approach to the problem of predicting the (average particle) distributions in inhomogeneities.
the DLEs, which are deterministic and computationally efficient, provide an efficient alternative to the MEs, which are stochastic and computationally intensive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a general method, applicable to systems of arbitrary dimension, for predicting particle distributions in in homogenous media.
, in the absence of steric constraints on diffusion, the steady-state particle distribution is determined only by the ratio of the particle hopping rates between neighboring domains.
we have developed an efficient computational method for predicting the particle distributions in systems of randomly diffusing, interacting particles in inhomogenous media.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of external fields or gradients, the steady-state particle distribution is governed by the particle hopping rates in the system.

, in the case of diffusion of randomly diffusing noninteracting particles in inhomogeneously structured media, the steady-state particle distribution is independent of the spatial structure of domains, and is instead determined by the ratio between the number of lattice site in each domain and the particle hopping rates between domains.

the particle distributions in systems with inhomogeneous particle diffusion are, in general, not governed by the local particle hopping rates, but rather by the average particle hopping rates in each domain.
